title: The stone that floated
hookLine: a Tamil saint tied to a stone sings Shiva's five syllables and floats to shore; the panchakshara as refuge
carry: om namah shivaya: shiva's name is a refuge
tomorrow: why does Ganesha get the first prayer, even at Shiva's puja?
last: ONE FACE OF GOD BECOMES YOUR ISHTA.

lines: THE KILN. THE POISON. THE ELEPHANT.
THROWN INTO THE SEA, HE SINGS.
cards: South India, more than thirteen hundred years ago. A poet-saint named Appar has angered a king. In the telling, the king tries everything.
Appar is shut in a burning kiln, and comes out cool. He's given poison, and it does nothing. An elephant is sent to crush him, and it bows instead.
So the king has him tied to a heavy stone and thrown into the sea. Sinking, Appar sings. Shiva's name, verse after verse.

teach.b: And the stone floats. It carries him to the shore like a raft. Tamil Shaiva tradition still sings the hymn he sang that day; each verse comes back to the same name: Namasivaya, his true companion.
In Sanskrit it's said Om Namah Shivaya. Take off the Om and count what's left: na, mah, shi, vaa, ya.

teach.h: FIVE SYLLABLES: I BOW TO SHIVA.
teach.b: Five syllables, so it's called the panchakshara, the five-syllable mantra. Om is the sound from day two. Namah means I bow.
Shivaya, to Shiva, and the name Shiva itself means kind, auspicious. So: Om, I bow to Shiva. Its words go back to a hymn in the Vedas.
Here's the teaching under Appar's story. For devotees of Shiva, these five syllables aren't only words about God.

teach.h: WHERE YOU GO WHEN ALL ELSE FAILS.
teach.b: Saying the name is itself a refuge, where you go when everything else has failed. Teachers read the syllables many ways.
In the Shaiva tradition of the south, they're matched to the five elements: earth, water, fire, air and space.

teach.h: OM NAMAH SHIVAYA: SHIVA'S NAME IS A REFUGE.
teach.b: Others hear Shiva's five acts: creating, keeping, dissolving, hiding and revealing. And there's a wordplay people love: namah heard as na mama, not mine. Bowing means you don't have to hold everything up yourself.
It's everywhere today: painted on trucks, carved over temple doors, sung all night at Shivaratri, whispered in traffic and in hospital waiting rooms. A bow, and a refuge.

how: Devotees of Shiva chant Om Namah Shivaya daily, often 108 times on a mala of rudraksha beads, and sing it through the night on Maha Shivaratri; Tamil Shaiva temples still sing Appar's hymns. It is widely chanted openly, though some lineages also give it formally at initiation.

o: a mantra with five Oms in it
a set of five daily prayers

games.q: match the story to the teaching.
p: the saint who sang in the sea

s: Om Namah Shivaya has five syllables counting the Om
take off the Om: na, mah, shi, vaa, ya. that's the five.
in the story, Appar's stone floated while he sang Shiva's name

games.q: a friend says Om Namah Shivaya is basically a lucky phrase, like knocking on wood. what fits today's teaching?
o: it's a bow: Om, I bow to Shiva. for devotees the name is a refuge, like Appar's in the sea.
yes, it's a lucky phrase that doesn't really mean anything.
it only counts if you say it exactly 108 times.
games.why: the five syllables say Om, I bow to Shiva. for Shiva's devotees, saying the name is itself a refuge.

practice: Japa means repeating a mantra and counting as you go; twenty-seven is a quarter of a mala, a string of prayer beads, so use beads if you have them, or touch each finger joint with your thumb.
On each out-breath, say softly and slowly, Om Namah Shivaya, and if you don't pray, just let it be sound, and count. At twenty-seven, stop, and sit in what's left.

wordCard.voice: Panchakshara, the five-syllable mantra: na, mah, shi, vaa, ya. Om, I bow to Shiva.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Om, I bow to Shiva. The panchakshara, five syllables after the Om.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: Om Namah Shivaya, Shiva's name is a refuge. Appar sang it sinking, and floated. See you tomorrow.
